entry: Canadian turboprop regional airliner. Introduced in 1984, the Dash 8 was developed from the Dash 7 with two more powerful Pratt & Whitney Canada PW100-series engines and improved cruise performance. Its four sizes included the Series 200, with 37–40 seats, and the Series 400, with 68–90. [[Boeing]] bought the manufacturer in 1986, followed by Bombardier in 1992 and Longview Aviation Capital in 2019, which revived the De Havilland Canada brand.

Four-engined British jet airliner, the world's first commercial jet. The Comet 1 prototype first flew in 1949, and the airliner entered service in 1952 with four [[Jet engine|turbojet engines]] in the wing roots. Within a year three Comets were lost in mid-flight accidents: two from structural failure caused by [[Fatigue (material)|metal fatigue]], and one from overstressing in severe weather. Design flaws led to extensive redesign. The redesigned Comet 4 debuted in 1958. The most extensive modification produced the Hawker Siddeley Nimrod maritime patrol aircraft, which remained in Royal Air Force service until 2011.

Pair of transformation rules in [[Propositional logic|propositional logic]] and [[Boolean algebra]]. Named after the 19th-century British mathematician Augustus De Morgan, they state that the negation of A and B equals not A or not B, and the negation of A or B equals not A and not B. In set theory, the complement of a union equals the [[Intersection (set theory)|intersection]] of the complements, and the reverse also holds. The laws allow conjunctions and disjunctions to be rewritten in terms of each other, which simplifies logic in [[Computer program|computer programs]] and digital circuits.

Astronomical treatise by [[Nicolaus Copernicus]] setting out a heliocentric model of the universe. Printed in [[Nuremberg]] in 1543, shortly before Copernicus's death, it offered an alternative to [[Ptolemy|Ptolemy's]] geocentric system, which had been widely accepted since ancient times. Copernicus placed the Sun at the center, with Earth and the other [[Planet|planets]] orbiting it. He had first outlined the system in an untitled manuscript, the *Commentariolus*, circulated among friends. Under strong pressure from the mathematician Georg Joachim Rheticus, he agreed to publication, and in 1542 a [[Trigonometry|trigonometry]] treatise drawn from the work's second book appeared under his name. The book is often linked to the start of the [[Scientific Revolution]].

Ancient Jewish biblical manuscripts, mostly from the Second Temple period. Discovered between 1946 and 1956 in the Qumran Caves near the [[Dead Sea]] in the [[West Bank]], they date from the 3rd century BCE to the 1st century CE and include the oldest surviving copies of books later included in Jewish and Christian biblical canons. Researchers have assembled 981 different manuscripts from 11 caves, and most of the roughly 15,000 scrolls and fragments are held in [[Jerusalem]]. The texts are mainly in Hebrew, with some in [[Aramaic]] and a few in Greek, written on [[Parchment|parchment]] and [[Papyrus|papyrus]]. About 40% copy the [[Hebrew Bible|Hebrew scriptures]], about 30% are Second Temple texts outside the Hebrew Bible, and the rest are sectarian works. [[Radiocarbon dating|Radiocarbon dating]] supports the dating.

Landlocked salt lake in the Jordan Rift Valley, bordered by [[Jordan]] to the east and [[Israel]] and the [[West Bank]] to the west. Its main tributary is the [[Jordan River]], and it has no outlet; at 304 m deep, it is the deepest hypersaline lake in the world. As of 2025 its surface lies 439.78 m below [[Sea level|sea level]], making its shores the lowest land-based elevation on Earth. With a salinity of 34.2% (2011), the water is about 9.6 times as salty as the ocean, so swimmers float, and few plants or animals survive. It was one of the world's first health resorts and has supplied products from [[Bitumen|bitumen]] for Egyptian mummification to [[Potash|potash]] for fertilizer. Its surface has shrunk from 1,050 sq km in 1930 to 605 sq km today.

American singer, actor and comedian, born Dino Paul Crocetti. Nicknamed "The King of Cool," he formed a nightclub act with comedian [[Jerry Lewis]] in 1946, billed as Martin and Lewis, which ended acrimoniously in 1956. As a solo performer he became one of the most popular acts in [[Las Vegas]] and a member of the Rat Pack with [[Frank Sinatra]] and [[Sammy Davis Jr.]] He hosted the television variety program *The Dean Martin Show* from 1965, and sold over 50 million records worldwide.

Japanese [[Manga|manga]] series by Tsugumi Ohba and Takeshi Obata. Serialized in *Weekly Shōnen Jump* from December 2003 to May 2006, it follows a high school student who finds a notebook in which writing a name causes that person's death. Light Yagami pursues a crime-free world under the alias Kira, while an elite police task force led by the detective L hunts him. A 37-episode [[Anime|anime]] series aired in 2006–07, and an American film was released on [[Netflix]] in 2017.

Desert valley in eastern [[California]], in the northern [[Mojave Desert]]. Lying mostly in Inyo County, near the [[Nevada]] border, it covers about 3,000 sq mi (7,800 sq km) and forms much of Death Valley National Park. A reading of 134 °F (56.7 °C) at Furnace Creek in 1913 is disputed, but the highest reliable temperature on Earth, 130 °F (54.4 °C), was recorded there in 2020 and 2021. The name dates from 1849–1850, when pioneers on their way to the California gold rush became lost in the valley; one member of the group died before they escaped.

American death metal band, formed in Altamonte Springs, Florida, in 1983. Guitarist Chuck Schuldiner founded the group, originally as Mantas, with Rick Rozz and Kam Lee. The lineup fluctuated, with Schuldiner its only consistent member. Regarded as a pioneering death metal band, Death released *Scream Bloody Gore* in 1987, among the first death metal records. The band disbanded after Schuldiner died of glioma and [[Pneumonia|pneumonia]] in December 2001.

Two-act [[Tragedy|tragedy]] by American playwright [[Arthur Miller]]. Set in late-1940s Brooklyn, it follows Willy Loman, a traveling salesman whose life is unraveling and who seems to be slipping into senility, through a montage of memories, dreams and arguments. Its themes include the American Dream, the nature of truth and infidelity. The play opened on Broadway on February 10, 1949, ran for 742 performances and won the [[Pulitzer Prize]] for Drama and the Tony Award for Best Play. It has been revived on Broadway five times, winning four Tony Awards for Best Revival. In 1999 critic John Lahr said that, with 11 million copies sold, it was "probably the most successful modern play ever published."

American actress, singer and dancer. Her breakout role was in *Singin' in the Rain* (1952), opposite [[Gene Kelly]]. She had a hit with the song "Tammy" from *Tammy and the Bachelor* (1957) and received an Academy Award nomination for Best Actress in *The Unsinkable Molly Brown* (1964). She voiced Charlotte in *Charlotte's Web* (1973), opened a dance studio, and pursued business ventures including a [[Las Vegas]] hotel and casino. Her daughter was actress [[Carrie Fisher]]. Reynolds died of a hemorrhagic [[Stroke|stroke]].

Free, general-purpose [[Operating system|operating system]], a Linux distribution. The volunteer Debian Project was founded by Ian Murdock on August 16, 1993. Debian is the second-oldest Linux distribution still in development, after Slackware, and forms the base of many others. Among Linux distributions it ranks second only to Ubuntu, a Debian derivative, with 16% of the overall market. Its emphasis on stability and long-term support has made it common on servers and embedded devices. Releases are named after characters in [[Toy Story]]. The current stable release, Trixie, appeared on August 9, 2025.

Payment card drawing funds directly from a linked [[Bank|bank]] account. Unlike a [[Credit card|credit card]], the money for a purchase must already be in the account and moves immediately to the merchant. Most debit cards relay a message to the bank to withdraw funds, although some hold stored value (prepaid) and others exist only as virtual card numbers for internet use. Debit cards usually also allow cash withdrawal from automated teller machines, and many new cards carry a chip for contactless use or PIN entry. In many countries debit cards have overtaken [[Cheque|cheques]] in volume or replaced them, though national systems often remain incompatible. The five major debit card networks are UnionPay, American Express, Discover, Mastercard and Visa.

Obligation to repay money borrowed or otherwise withheld from a creditor. A debtor may be a [[Sovereign state|sovereign state]], local government, company or individual, and commercial debt is generally governed by contract terms for repaying principal and interest. [[Loan|Loans]], [[Bond (finance)|bonds]], notes and [[Mortgage|mortgages]] are all types of debt. Repayment may fall due in full at maturity, be amortized over the term, or leave a final balloon payment. If a debt is secured by collateral, the creditor may repossess it, and serious defaults can lead to [[Bankruptcy|bankruptcy]]. Individuals commonly owe mortgages, car loans, credit card debt and [[Income tax|income taxes]]. The term entered English in the late 13th century from Old French, which took it from Latin *debere*, meaning to owe.

Complete separation of the head from the body. It is invariably fatal to humans and vertebrate animals, because it cuts off the brain's oxygenated blood supply. Beheading, the deliberate decapitation of a person, may be carried out with an ax, sword or knife, or by a [[Guillotine|guillotine]]. [[Saudi Arabia]] and [[Yemen]] permit beheading under national law, and under [[Sharia]], which applies only to Muslims, it is a legal punishment in Zamfara State, [[Nigeria]]. In France the [[French Revolution]] made beheading the only legal method of execution for all criminals. The practice has also become associated with [[Terrorism|terrorism]].

Crustacean in the large order Decapoda, within the class [[Malacostraca]]. Decapods include [[Crab|crabs]], [[Lobster|lobsters]], [[Crayfish|crayfish]] and [[Shrimp|shrimp]], and most are [[Scavenger|scavengers]]. The name, from Greek for ten and foot, refers to ten legs, called pereiopods, on the last five thoracic segments. The order contains nearly 15,000 living species in about 2,700 genera, and nearly half are crabs. Decapods can have as many as 38 appendages, and the order is divided into two suborders, Dendrobranchiata (prawns) and Pleocyemata, according to the structure of gills and legs and the way larvae develop. The earliest fossils date to the [[Devonian]].

Combined athletics event of ten [[Track and field]] events, contested over two consecutive days. Winners are decided by points scored in each event rather than by place. The events include the 100 meters, [[Long jump]], [[Shot put]], [[High jump]], 400 meters, 110 meters hurdles, [[Discus throw]], [[Pole vault]], [[Javelin throw]] and 1500 meters. The name is formed on the analogy of pentathlon, a contest at the ancient Greek Olympics. The modern decathlon first appeared at the 1912 Stockholm Olympics, where [[Jim Thorpe]] won and was told by Gustav V of Sweden, "Sir, you are the world's greatest athlete." The men's world record is 9,126 points, set by Kevin Mayer of France in 2018. Women typically compete in the heptathlon.

Plateau forming the bulk of the Deccan Peninsula in western, central and southern India. It covers about 422,000 sq km (163,000 sq mi) and is bounded by the Eastern and [[Western Ghats]], which block rain-bearing winds, leaving the region drier than the coast. Its average elevation is about 600 m, and it slopes gently east toward the [[Bay of Bengal]], so major rivers such as the Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri flow that way. The northwestern [[Deccan Traps]] are layers of basalt from a massive volcanic eruption at the end of the Cretaceous period. In the later Middle Ages the [[Vijayanagara Empire]] held the lower plateau and the [[Deccan sultanates]] the upper. The area was under [[British Raj]] control for nearly two centuries before Indian independence in 1947.

Large igneous province of west-central India, among the largest volcanic features on Earth. Its many layers of flood basalt are more than 2 km thick, cover about 500,000 sq km and have a volume of about 1 million cubic km. The eruptions occurred over 600,000 to 800,000 years, between about 66.3 and 65.6 million years ago, spanning the [[Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary]]. The eruptions are now generally considered to have played a minor role at most in the Cretaceous–Paleogene mass extinction, with the Chicxulub impact regarded as the primary cause. The province is thought to have been produced largely by the [[Réunion]] hotspot, which created the Mascarene Islands.

Historiographical term for five medieval Persianate Muslim kingdoms of the [[Deccan Plateau]]: Ahmadnagar, Berar, Bidar, Bijapur and Golconda. They emerged after the Bahmani Sultanate disintegrated; Ahmadnagar declared independence in 1490, followed by Bijapur and Berar that year, Bidar around 1492 and Golconda in 1512. Their founders were of diverse origins: Bidar's by a Georgian slave and Golconda's by a slave of Iranian Turkmen origin. All based their legitimacy on succeeding the Bahmani Sultanate and used its coins. Although often rivals, the sultanates allied against the [[Vijayanagara Empire]] at the Battle of Talikota in 1565, which destroyed the city of Vijayanagara. The [[Mughal Empire]] took Berar in 1596 and Ahmadnagar between 1616 and 1636, and [[Aurangzeb]] conquered Golconda and Bijapur in 1686–87.

Last [[Dacians|Dacian]] king (r. 87–106). He fought three wars against the [[Roman Empire]] under two emperors. After raiding south across the [[Danube]], he defeated a Roman invasion under [[Domitian]], killing its commander Cornelius Fuscus, and secured a period of independence. He was crowned king after the aging Duras abdicated, and the Roman historian Cassius Dio called him a shrewd commander and a worthy antagonist of the Romans for a long time. [[Trajan]] invaded Dacia and defeated Decebalus in 102, after which he remained a client king. A final Roman invasion in 105 was followed by the destruction of the Dacian capital Sarmizegetusa in 106, and Decebalus died by [[Suicide|suicide]] to avoid capture.

Twelfth and final month of the year in the Julian and Gregorian calendars, with 31 days. Its name derives from Latin *decem*, meaning ten, because it was the tenth month of Romulus's calendar, c. 750 BC, which began in March. It is the first month of winter in the Northern Hemisphere, when the [[Winter solstice]] falls, and the first month of summer in the Southern Hemisphere. Its birth flower is the narcissus, and its birthstones are turquoise, zircon and tanzanite.

Distribution of planning and decision-making away from a central authority, applied to organizations, politics, law, [[Public administration|public administration]], technology, economics and money. The word *centralisation* came into use in France in 1794, and *décentralisation* in the 1820s. In the early 20th century, a decentralist movement in the United States opposed the concentration of economic wealth and political power in large-scale industry. In government, decentralization usually means devolving administrative or fiscal authority to subnational governments. In technology it appears in distributed systems such as [[Blockchain|blockchain]]. The anarchist theorist [[Pierre-Joseph Proudhon]] summed up his political ideas as federation or decentralization. Leopold Kohr's 1957 book *The Breakdown of Nations* influenced E. F. Schumacher's *Small Is Beautiful* (1973).

Logarithmic unit equal to one tenth of a bel, expressing the ratio of two power or root-power quantities. A tenfold change in power is 10 dB, and a tenfold change in amplitude is 20 dB. Two signals whose levels differ by one decibel have a power ratio of about 1.26. The unit originated in early 20th-century telephone measurement at the Bell System, and the bel is named after [[Alexander Graham Bell]]. The decibel is most widely used for sound in [[Acoustics]], and for [[Amplifier|amplifier]] gains, signal losses and [[Signal-to-noise ratio|signal-to-noise ratios]] in [[Electronics]].
